observation: Sketch of the approach: Bamiyan, 200 li to the snow mountains, over the 黑嶺 into Kapiśa (Begram); "4000 li around → 1000 km!"
assessment: 4000 li ≈ 1000 km is the same scale the route model finds (≈0.24 km per li straight-line, 0.29–0.32 km by road).

observation: Is the 曷邏怙羅僧伽藍 (大城東南三十餘里) at Mes Aynak? "30 li (15 km?)"; "How far is Mes Aynak from Begram?"; "He may not have stopped in Mes Aynak."
assessment: Does not fit the text. 大城東南三十餘里 is c. 7–10 km at the route model's scale (0.24 km per li straight-line, 0.29–0.32 by road; the sketch's 15 km assumes 0.5 km per li); Mes Aynak is c. 82 km straight-line from Begram. Kuwayama (2000, p. 26) identifies the Rāhula monastery with the standing stūpa Borj-e Kafir, "the one and only site" south of Begram, which supports the study's Kafir Qaleh; and he places Kabul and the Logar side in 弗栗恃薩儻那, not Kapiśa (p. 57). Mes Aynak is a major Buddhist site of the period but not the Rāhula monastery; Xuanzang names nothing there.

observation: 霫蔽多伐剌祠城: "Śvetāśvatara?"
assessment: Already proposed by Kuwayama: "Svetavara, probably a corrupt form of Svetasvatara", the base of the Pāśupatas of Kapiśa in his reading of 塗灰 (2000, p. 27; 1972, p. 46). He places the town at Tapa Skandar near Sarai Khwaja, where the Kyoto mission found the marble Umā-Maheśvara in 1970 (2000, pp. 26–27; 1972, p. 54). That is c. 50 km S of Begram, long for 40 li; the study's Tatarānzar (Foucher, c. 12 km) fits the distance but has no Śaiva find. Recorded as an alternative.

observation: 阿路猱山 30 li S of 霫蔽多伐剌祠城 (sketch 2).
assessment: Kuwayama (2000, pp. 27, 29, 36) takes the 阿路猱山 as Mount Aruṇa, a Sūrya cult site, and identifies it with the 'Trois Sanctuaires' of Khair Khana N of Kabul. New to the study, which had no location.

observation: From Kapiśa Xuanzang goes east into 濫波; the next country, 那揭羅曷, is Jalalabad (the sketch writes "Lamghān or … Laghman / Jalalabad").
assessment: Agrees with the study: Laghman = 濫波 (Lampāka, 02.02); Jalalabad = 那揭羅曷 (Nagarahāra, 02.03).

observation: Songyun's 善特山 (= 檀特山 of the Weishu 102, Xuanzang's 彈多落迦山; Mekha-Sanda per Nagasawa) has a 護塔神濕婆仙 who drives the monastery's donkeys, and a 廟 of the 濕婆仙 built by the king where the 濕婆仙 swept ash in place of a novice: Buddhist and Śaiva (perhaps ash-smearers) side by side. Beal (1869, p. xcix) missed the Śaiva reference. 挽 may mean "moan" as well as "pull".
source_note: This is probably a reference to the Pāśupata practice
assessment: Confirmed, and anticipated by Nagasawa (東洋文庫 法顕伝・宋雲行紀), who translates 濕婆仙 as the god Śiva (p. 192) and suggests that 除灰 'removing ash' may be an error for 塗灰 'smearing ash', linking it with the ash-smearing worshippers of Śiva (p. 201). Beal (1869, p. 196; 1884, I p. xcix) renders 濕婆仙 as "the Rishi Uh-po (Oupa? conf. Oupagupta)" and misses Śiva. Caveat: this is the Vessantara mountain, and the jātaka's king of 葉波國 is called 湿波 (Nagasawa p. 200), so the stūpa-guarding 濕婆仙 might echo the jātaka; but 仙, the ash and the royal shrine with a painted, gilded image point to a Śaiva figure. A Śiva shrine inside the Buddhist complex c. 520, a century before Xuanzang.

observation: The Bhīmā hill (Karamar) with its 大自在天祠 served by 塗灰外道 may be the same place as Songyun's Śaiva shrine; Xuanzang's ash-smearers at Mizutani pp. 94–96.
source_note: This is probably a reference…; 外道 by 玄奘 (l. 9); Pāṇini note
assessment: Kuwayama (1972, p. 46) also reads the Bhīmā hill's 大自在天祠 with its 塗灰外道 as a Pāśupata cult site. Songyun's 善特山 (Daṇḍaloka, 20 li NE of Varuṣa) and the Bhīmā hill (50 li NE) are different places in Xuanzang's account, but close (c. 7–9 km apart), so a Śaiva presence in these hills is attested by both pilgrims.

observation: Pāṇini's birthplace (Mizutani 4.19, p. 96): Śalātura.
source_note: 玄奘 Xuanzang refers to the birthplace of Pāṇini
assessment: Agrees with the study (02.04.19, *śalātura).

observation: Uḍḍiyāna's monks practise 禁呪, vidyā/dhāraṇī (Mizutani p. 100 n. 5); more than ten deva temples.
source_note: 玄奘 Xuanzang refers to the birthplace of Pāṇini
assessment: Agrees with the study's coding (10+ deva temples); the 禁呪 practice is recorded here as a characteristic of the local Buddhism.

observation: 白衣外道 at Siṃhapura = Śvetāmbara (Mizutani p. 121); Xuanzang "could not, like us, tell the difference between Jainism and Buddhism".
assessment: Agrees: the study codes Śvetāmbara and Digambara at the site of the founder's first sermon (03.04.03); the country description itself names no religion.

observation: After the Kṛtya story (外道天祠，特留意焉): "there were more Hindus than Buddhists" in Kashmir.
assessment: Agrees with the study's "Brahmanical" for Kashmir.

observation: I cannot identify Chiniyari near Amritsar identified as this place.
assessment: The study also rates Cīnabhukti disputed.

observation: Mayūrapura (Haridwar): 大天祠 coded Ś.
assessment: 大天祠 is usually translated "great deva temple"; read as 大天 = Mahādeva it is a Śiva temple. Both readings are now recorded in the religion coding (other: Mahādeva?), without tagging the place Śaiva on the map.

observation: Brahmapura: "Brahmapura?/Bālakumā[ra]pura?"; Pauri Garhwal / Srinagar.
assessment: The study now places the capital in Kumaon (Talesvara plates, Lakhanpur), not Srinagar. "Bālakumārapura" is a question in the note's heading, without a source. It does not fit the transcription: 婆羅吸摩補羅 renders bra-hma-pura closely, and kumāra would need characters such as 鳩摩羅. Brahmapura is also attested locally, in the Talesvara plates issued from a royal Brahmapura in Kumaon. Not adopted.

observation: Ahicchatra's 塗灰之侶: "Look for Ahicchatra in Liz's Mapping the Pāśupata landscape."
assessment: Cecil (2020) does not use Xuanzang; her only Ahichatrapura is the Bijolia inscription's town in the Ananta region of Rajasthan (p. 108, n. 12), not the Rohilkhand Ahicchattra. Nothing to add from her book.

observation: Ayodhyā: "Vasubandhu worked and died here and we do not know the location."
assessment: Recorded; no identification proposed.

observation: The 那羅延天祠 north of the Ganges "might be … one in Revelganj"; Xuanzang "is aware of Nārāyaṇa".
assessment: Agrees with the study (probably Revelganj; coded Vaiṣṇava).

observation: Vaiśālī: many Digambaras.
assessment: Agrees with the study.

observation: 露形外道 on Vipula hill: "Mention of Digambaras".
assessment: The study had this sentence under the next site (09.02.11a, the Pippala cave), so Vipula itself was not tagged Jain. Corrected (religion_zz_user.tsv).

observation: Nālandā: "Nothing whatsoever about followers of other religions."
assessment: The founding legend has a Nirgrantha diviner (時有善占尼乾外道), which the study codes; otherwise agreed.

observation: The smoke and mist of the 伊爛拏山 (含吐煙霞): volcanic activity, or the hot spring Sita Kund? Cites the Life (慈恩傳) on the route.
assessment: Fits the study's note: Vivien and the gazetteers favour the hot-spring range at Monghyr, where Sita Kund lies. Volcanism is not attested for the historical period.

observation: Puṇḍravardhana's 露形尼乾: "He probably means Digambara Jains but there were also many Hindu artifacts at the site apparently."
assessment: Agrees (Jain-Digambara).

observation: Faxian's 達嚫 and 波羅越 cave monastery are described almost exactly as Xuanzang's 跋邏末羅耆釐. 鴿 (pigeon) comes from taking parvata as pārāvata. Bhrāmaragiri may have been reconstructed from the gloss 黒蜂, and 黒蜂 may be a corruption of 黒峰 ("black peak").
source_note: 法顕 and Dakṣiṇa…; 法顕 dakṣiṇakosala, etc.
assessment: The Faxian–Xuanzang match is also Mizutani's, and the two descriptions (a mountain hollowed into a five-storeyed monastery, water led round the storeys, light let in through cut windows) support it. On the name: 跋邏末羅 (MC roughly *bat-la-mat-la) transcribes bhramara independently of the gloss, and 黑蜂 'black bee' is the standard gloss of bhramara, so the Sanskrit is not only a back-formation from 黑蜂; an emendation to 黑峰 would leave the transcription unexplained. The Arang inscription's Bhaṃgara-pavata (bhṛṅga, also 'bee'; 10.12.05 note) agrees with the bee reading. Faxian's 波羅越 'pigeon' (pārāvata) may well come from parvata, as suggested, which would make his name a different word for the same place. The gloss 黑峰 'black peak' is Nagasawa's (p. 128: 'Bhrāmara-giri, 黒峰山'); Taishō and CBETA read 黑蜂, with no variant noted. Nagasawa takes Faxian's 達嚫 as Dakṣiṇa, location unknown, 200 yojanas S of Kauśāmbī (p. 127), compares Xuanzang's five-storeyed Bhramaragiri, and cites Huichao's rock monastery built for Nāgārjuna (p. 128).

observation: Pulakeśin II is named, so is the capital Badami or Nasik? "Did Xuanzang actually visit Badami?"; header gives "capital Nashik".
source_note: Xuanzang 玄奘 on Konkan and Mahāraṭa; 外道 by 玄奘 (l. 198)
assessment: The study's note favours Nasik (bearing to Ajanta; Chalukya grants from Nasik district; the capital "west of a great river" fits the Godāvarī). Badami was the dynastic capital, but Xuanzang's data do not point to it.

observation: If Faxian's cave monastery is the same as Xuanzang's in Kosala, and some take Faxian's to be Ajanta, then the Ajanta identification needs rethinking.
assessment: Not affected. If Faxian's 波羅越 is Xuanzang's Bhramaragiri in Kosala (10.12.05), Faxian does not describe Ajanta; but the Ajanta identification of 阿折羅伽藍 rests on Xuanzang's own account (the mountain on the east border of Mahārāṣṭra, a monastery founded by the arhat Acala, a great vihāra with sculptured stone walls and stone elephants at the gate), on the bearing from Nasik, and on the cave inscription naming the sthavira Acala (Ajanta Cave 26; known from Burgess and Bhagwanlal Indraji 1881, not among the sources coded here). The two descriptions differ in kind, so the Ajanta identification stands.

observation: Mālava's capital: Ujjain or Ahmedabad?
assessment: The study moved Mālava to central Gujarat (Kaira/Ahmedabad), so the second option.

observation: Jejākabhukti: "hard to identify; Bundelkhand? capital possibly Khajuraho?"
assessment: Mizutani's first option; the study leaves it undecided (Eran reconstruction in 11.13).

observation: Maheśvarapura: Shivpuri or Mandla?
assessment: The study keeps Gwalior and drops Mandla (off the bearing). From the study's Eran capital for 11.13, Gwalior lies due north at c. 235 km, matching 900 li; Shivpuri lies NNW at c. 155 km, short of 900 li. Shivpuri is recorded as an alternative within the same region, weaker on distance.

observation: Atyanabakela: the capital 朅䶩濕伐羅 "should definitely be Koṭīśvara (Koteshwar)"; 翅羅 transcribes -kila (cf. 倶翅羅 = kokila in the 一切經音義; the 悉曇要訣); new 20th-c. port discoveries should be re-examined; Debal (Lambrick 1964: 148); Bhambore.
assessment: Possible on location, weak on the name, and not new: Cunningham already put the capital at Kotesar on the Kori mouth (AGI pp. 347–8), Watters calls that restoration "quite impossible" (II p. 257), and Lambrick (Sind, p. 148; the 1986 reprint is textually identical with 1964) prefers the delta with Debal as the capital. 朅 (MC *khjat) suits Kacch-/Khaj- better than Koṭi-. The 翅羅 = kila argument concerns the country name, not the capital. In favour of the Kutch side, al-Bīrūnī puts the Indus's eastern mouth "in the province of Kacch at a place called Sindhu-sāgara" (Sachau I p. 260), and the Skandapurāṇa's Śaṅkukarṇa with its Sthūleśvara liṅga lies at the Sindhu–ocean confluence (SP IV p. 57; Bakker places it at Banbhore, SP IV p. 55 n. 133). A great Śiva shrine at the Indus mouth fits this country's 大自在天祠 served by ash-smearers (塗灰外道). Low to medium confidence; Mirchandani 1969 (JIH 47: 237–51) treats this capital too and should be read. Mirchandani puts the country in Las Bela (the Arabs' Armābel), with the capital at Gondakahar 11 miles NW of Bela (JIH 45, 1967, pp. 322–30), and reads its name as Kiteśvara < Kitaveśvara (JIH 47, 1969, p. 250): a fourth candidate, west of the Indus, resting on the Chachnāma's Armābel rather than on the name.

observation: Laṅgala: could the name be Lākula? Capital 窣菟黎濕伐羅 = Sthūleśvara, a tīrtha (with Śaṅkukarṇa) in the Skandapurāṇa (vol. 4 p. 57; 73.57) and Śivadharmaśāstra 12; al-Bīrūnī's coastal Loharānī (Sachau I p. 260) and "tawwaleshar"; al-Daibal = Devālaya = Debal/Bhambore; Niśvāsamukha 3.12–13 (sindhusāgara); Cunningham's Lakūra "misinformed"; or simply a port town on the coast, as Xuanzang's directions suggest.
assessment: Name supported, location contradicted. 窣菟黎濕伐羅 is a very good transcription of sthūleśvara (窣 as in 窣堵波); Watters already suggested "sthul or sthur" (II p. 257) and Mirchandani (JIH 47, 1969, p. 247) proposed Sthūleśvara outright, but his only Indian attestation was the Devī Bhāgavata's pīṭha Sthūlakeśvara, which he thought possibly fictitious; he placed the city at Kasarkand in Persian Makran (p. 244) and derived Laṅgala from lāṅgala 'palm' (p. 246). The Skandapurāṇa and Śivadharmaśāstra evidence in K. Harimoto's note is new to the question. But the Skandapurāṇa puts the liṅga Sthūleśvara at Śaṅkukarṇa, at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean (SP 73.57; SP IV pp. 10, 57), which Bakker locates at Banbhore near Karachi — Atyanabakela's region, not 2000 li west of it. Al-Bīrūnī's Tawalleshar (Sachau I p. 208; cf. Taneshar = Sthāneśvara, I p. 199) may be the same name but lies on the coast east of Daibal; Loharānī is the port at the western Indus mouth (I pp. 205, 260), not a candidate. So either a second Sthūleśvara existed on the Makran coast, or the name belongs with the delta and Xuanzang's Laṅgala sequence needs rethinking. Lākula is unsupported (Cecil p. 14: lakula is Lakulīśa's club); Cunningham's Lakūra rests on changing W to NW (AGI p. 356). Open question; a strong lead.

observation: Persia's capital 蘇剌薩儻那: Surasthāna(?).
assessment: Recorded.

observation: Avaṇḍa: Khairpur or Brahmanabad; "al-Bīrūnī's … al-Mansura?"
assessment: Unsupported as a name, possible as a site. Al-Bīrūnī says al-Mansūra was Bahmanwa renamed after the conquest (Sachau I p. 21; Brahmanavāta, I p. 316); it was founded c. 744–74 (Cunningham pp. 310–11), a century after Xuanzang. Cunningham already equated Avaṇḍa with Bahmanwa/Brahmanabad, the site al-Mansūra was built on, which is the study's present view. Lambrick instead puts Avaṇḍa at Badah, S of Larkana (pp. 149–50): a new alternative for the study. Mirchandani (ABORI 57, 1976, pp. 86 n. 17, 90; JIH 45, 1967) puts Avaṇḍa in Kachhi (Kachh Gandāva), NW of Sindh, with its capital at Gandāva.

observation: 䅳那天: "Nobody appears to know who 䅳那天 is."
assessment: Kuwayama (2000, pp. 29–33) identifies 䅳那天 with the Zhun 順 of the Suishu's 漕國, whose statue stood on 葱嶺; he argues the Zhun cult held Mount Aruṇa first and left for Zābulistān (the 䅳那呬羅山) between 606 and 629, when a Sūrya group took the mountain. The god himself remains unidentified in Indian terms.

observation: The 塗炭外道 in Khotan's foundation legend is an ash-smearer (the note has "Pāśupata … for ashes").
assessment: Agrees with the study (coded Pasupata, displayed as ash-smearers).

observation: Potalaka: location unknown; somewhere on the Tamil coast; the port NE of the mountain could be Pondicherry (Arikamedu). Avalokiteśvara appearing as 自在天 or a 塗灰外道: "imitating God? Cf. Hans' article".
assessment: The study follows Mizutani (Podiyil/Pāpanāsam range, or legendary). Arikamedu is recorded as a candidate for the port only; the text puts the port NE of the mountain on the sea route to Siṃhala, and Arikamedu is a Roman-period port, not shown to be active in the 7th c. "Hans' article" is Bakker, Monuments of Hope, Gloom, and Glory in the Age of the Hunnic Wars (Gonda Lecture 2016, publ. 2017), p. 15: after Eltschinger 2014, the Kāraṇḍavyūha has Avalokiteśvara prophesy that Maheśvara will be the creator in the Kali age — the Buddhist view in which Avalokiteśvara can appear in Śiva's form.

observation: (Not in the notes; from the Mirchandani articles the notes point to.) Mirchandani argues that Xuanzang's 信度 lay W of the Indus opposite Multan, with the capital 毘苫婆補羅 near Mithankot.
source_note: Mirchandani 1976 (pointed to by the Laṅgala note)
assessment: Recorded as an alternative to Alor (Mizutani: Upper Sind, Sukkur district). It rests on Xuanzang's bearings from Multan and from Gurjara and on the Life's 700 li from Avaṇḍa; the study's route model has not been run on it.

observation: Afghanistan.pptx (Philippe Marquis, "Afghanistan an update", 2020; linked from the note "mountain _____ mountain") quotes Xuanzang on 提謂城 (50 li NW of the capital) and 波利城 (40 li N of it) and the Kāśyapa stūpa 70 li W, and marks three sites on a map of the Balkh oasis with Google Earth images.

assessment: The slides do not connect Mes Aynak with Xuanzang.
